characters.name: David
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around final royal authority — securing succession and settling old debts (Joab, Shimei) before death.

genealogy.note: Only relationships stated within 1 Kings are asserted here (1:11-31, 2:13-25). David's fuller genealogy (son of Jesse) and full wife/son list are established in 1-2 Samuel, not re-derived from those books for this entry.

funFacts: Reigned a stated total of 40 years — 7 in Hebron, 33 in Jerusalem (2:11).
Kept warm in old age by Abishag the Shunammite, though the text explicitly states 'the king knew her not' (1:1-4).
His deathbed charge to Solomon (2:1-9) instructs mercy to Barzillai's sons but settles old scores with Joab and Shimei — not a purely peaceful farewell.

verses.note: 'Now king David was old and stricken in years' — opens the book with his decline.
David swears to Bathsheba that Solomon, not Adonijah, will reign.
David's final charge to Solomon: keep the LORD's statutes, then deal with Joab and Shimei.

characters.name: Bathsheba
characters.perkNote: Secures Solomon's succession by petitioning David directly.

genealogy.note: Only her role as Solomon's mother/David's wife within 1 Kings is asserted; her introduction and prior marriage (2 Samuel 11) are not re-derived here.

funFacts: Later, in 1 Kings 2:13-25, she unknowingly relays Adonijah's fatal request for Abishag to Solomon.

verses.note: Goes in to David per Nathan's plan and reminds him of his oath that Solomon would reign.
Solomon rises, bows to her, and sets a throne at his right hand — 'the king's mother.'

characters.name: Nathan the prophet
characters.perkNote: Counsels the plan that secures Solomon's throne.

genealogy.note: Prior history with David (2 Samuel) not re-derived; only his role in 1 Kings 1 is asserted.

funFacts: Devises the plan for Bathsheba to speak to David first, then enters himself to confirm it (1:11-27).

verses.note: Instructs Bathsheba to go in to David about Adonijah's self-proclaimed kingship.
Confirms Bathsheba's report to David and questions whether Adonijah's kingship was ordered by the king.

characters.name: Zadok the priest
characters.perkNote: Anoints Solomon king at Gihon, sealing the succession.

children: Azariah the son of Zadok (4:2, per that officer's own entry)
genealogy.note: Named as father of the officer Azariah in 4:2; not the same man as Azariah the son of Nathan in 4:5 (see that entry's collision note).

funFacts: Sides with Solomon while Abiathar the priest sides with Adonijah — the priesthood itself splits over the succession (1:7-8).

verses.note: Anoints Solomon with the horn of oil out of the tabernacle at Gihon.
His son Azariah is listed among Solomon's officers as 'the priest.'

characters.name: Adonijah
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around premature self-promotion — high initial claim, collapses fast.

genealogy.note: Called 'the son of Haggith' (1:5) — Haggith is named only as his mother's name within 1 Kings, no further detail given here.

funFacts: 'His father had not displeased him at any time in saying, Why hast thou done so?' (1:6) — the text explicitly notes David never disciplined him.
His fatal request to marry Abishag (2:13-25) is read by Solomon as a renewed bid for the throne, since possessing a king's concubine implied a claim to his position.

verses.note: 'Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, I will be king.'
Holds a sacrificial feast at En-rogel, inviting his brothers and Judah's men but not Solomon, Nathan, or Benaiah.
Solomon has him executed by Benaiah after his request for Abishag.

characters.name: Joab
characters.perkNote: Backs the losing succession bid; executed for it.

genealogy.note: Called 'the captain of the host' (1:7, 2:5); his earlier career (2 Samuel) is not re-derived here — only his role in 1 Kings is asserted.

funFacts: David's charge to Solomon (2:5-6) specifically cites Joab's killing of Abner and Amasa 'in peace' as blood David wants avenged.
Flees to the tabernacle and grasps the horns of the altar for sanctuary, but Solomon has Benaiah kill him there anyway (2:28-34).

verses.note: Follows Adonijah, alongside Abiathar the priest.
Executed by Benaiah at the altar on Solomon's order.

characters.name: Abiathar the priest
characters.perkNote: Backs the losing succession bid; loses the priesthood but is spared execution.

genealogy.note: Distinct from Zadok; his earlier priestly history (1 Samuel) is not re-derived here.

funFacts: Solomon spares his life specifically because he 'bare the ark of the Lord God before David' and shared David's afflictions (2:26) — mercy grounded in prior loyalty, not the succession fight itself.
His removal is explicitly said to fulfil the LORD's earlier word against the house of Eli (2:27).

verses.note: Follows Adonijah.
Banished to Anathoth and removed from the priesthood, sparing his life.

characters.name: Abishag the Shunammite
characters.perkNote: Her requested hand becomes the pretext for Adonijah's execution.

genealogy.note: Attached here (rather than to David) because her narrative significance plays out through Adonijah's request for her in 2:13-25, which triggers his death.

funFacts: Chosen to be brought to David for warmth in his old age; the text specifies she was 'a fair damsel' sought out of all the coasts of Israel (1:3-4).

verses.note: Brought to minister to and lie with the aged David; the text states he 'knew her not.'
Adonijah asks Bathsheba to request her as a wife from Solomon.

characters.name: Solomon
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around wisdom-driven discernment and administration; also the book's clearest fall-from-grace arc.

spouses: many others (700 wives, 300 concubines per 11:3, not individually named in 1 Kings)
genealogy.note: 11:3 gives numeric totals for wives/concubines without individual names, aside from Pharaoh's daughter and Naamah the Ammonitess (mother of Rehoboam, 14:21) — only these two are used as named individuals here.

funFacts: Asks God for 'an understanding heart to judge thy people' rather than riches or long life (3:9), and is granted both wisdom and unmatched wealth (3:11-13).
Wrote (per the text's own claim) 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs, and spoke of trees, beasts, fowl, creeping things, and fishes (4:32-33).
His heart is explicitly said to have been 'turned away after other gods' by his many foreign wives in his old age (11:4).

verses.note: Judges between the two harlots over the living child — the episode that establishes his reputation for wisdom.
Begins building the house of the LORD in the 480th year after the Exodus, his 4th regnal year.
His foreign wives turn his heart to other gods; the LORD announces the kingdom will be torn from his son (but not from Solomon himself, for David's sake).
Reigned 40 years over Israel; died and was succeeded by Rehoboam.

characters.name: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada
characters.perkNote: Executes Solomon's judgments and rises to command the host.

genealogy.note: Prior exploits (2 Samuel 23) not re-derived; only his role in 1 Kings is asserted.

funFacts: Personally kills Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei son of Gera on Solomon's orders (2:25, 2:34, 2:46).
Replaces Joab as captain of the host (2:35).

verses.note: Supports Solomon's anointing, escorting him to Gihon.
Kills Joab and is made captain of the host in his place.
Listed among Solomon's chief officers, over the host.

characters.name: Shimei the son of Gera
characters.perkNote: Confined by royal decree; executed for breaking its terms.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: this Shimei (son of Gera, a Benjamite, executed by Solomon in 2:36-46) is a different man from Shimei the son of Elah, one of Solomon's twelve district officers over Benjamin (4:18) — same book, two different men both connected to the tribe of Benjamin.

funFacts: Solomon confines him to Jerusalem on pain of death (2:36-38); he is executed three years later for leaving the city to retrieve runaway servants from Gath (2:39-46), not for any new offense against Solomon directly.

verses.note: Solomon commands him to build a house in Jerusalem and never cross the brook Kidron on pain of death.
Executed by Benaiah for breaking the oath by going to Gath.

characters.name: Hiram, king of Tyre
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around foreign alliance and trade — supplies materials, but the relationship sours.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: this is Hiram the KING of Tyre, a distinct person from Hiram the bronze craftsman of chapter 7 (see that entry) — the book uses the same name for two entirely different men in two different roles.

funFacts: Was 'ever a lover of David' (5:1), and the alliance continues into Solomon's reign.
When Solomon gives him twenty cities in Galilee as payment, Hiram is displeased and calls the land 'Cabul' (9:11-13) — the alliance ends on a sour, unflattering note, not a purely triumphant one.
Sends a joint navy with Solomon to Ophir, returning 420 talents of gold (9:26-28).

verses.note: Supplies cedar and fir trees for the Temple in exchange for wheat and oil; the two kings make a league.
Receives twenty cities in Galilee from Solomon, is displeased with them, and calls the land Cabul.

characters.name: Hiram (the craftsman)
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around fine bronze craftsmanship for the Temple.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: distinct from Hiram the king of Tyre. Per 1 Kings 7:13-14 (KJV wording only — not the 2 Chronicles 'Huram his father' phrasing), he was 'a widow's son of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in brass.' His mother was of Naphtali; his late father was a Tyrian bronzeworker — no compound name 'Huram-abi' appears anywhere in 1 Kings.

funFacts: Cast the two bronze pillars Jachin and Boaz (7:15-22) and the 'molten sea' — a massive bronze basin ten cubits across, resting on twelve oxen (7:23-26).

verses.note: Introduced as a widow's son of Naphtali, sent for from Tyre by Solomon; 'filled with wisdom and understanding and cunning to work all works in brass.'
Finishes all the bronze work for the house of the LORD.

characters.name: The Temple Dedication and the LORD's Covenant Response
characters.deliveredBy: Solomon (dedication prayer, spoken at the altar before the congregation, 8:22-53); the LORD (covenant response, given to Solomon in a night vision, 9:1-9)
characters.purpose: Establishes that the newly built Temple's holiness and the LORD's continued presence in it are conditioned on covenant obedience by Solomon and Israel, not automatic or permanent. The LORD's response explicitly warns that disobedience will cause Israel to be cut off from the land and the Temple itself to become 'a proverb and a byword' among the nations (9:6-9) — a warning that frames the rest of the book's arc toward division and idolatry as a fulfillment already foretold at the height of Solomon's glory.

verses.note: The cloud fills the house of the LORD at its dedication, so that the priests could not stand to minister.
Solomon's dedication prayer, including petitions for Israel when they sin, are defeated, suffer famine, or are carried captive to a foreign land.
The LORD's response: hallows the house, but warns that turning to other gods will cause Israel to be cut off and the house cast out of His sight.

characters.name: The Queen of Sheba
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around testing and confirming wisdom through hard questions.

genealogy.note: No personal name is given in 1 Kings; 'Sheba' names her kingdom/people, not a father. Identification with any later-named figure is not made by the text itself.

funFacts: Comes 'to prove him with hard questions' (10:1) and finds that 'the half was not told' her of Solomon's wisdom and wealth (10:6-7).
Gives Solomon 120 talents of gold, spices in great abundance, and precious stones (10:10) — the largest single gift of spices the text says Israel ever received (10:10).

verses.note: Comes to test Solomon with hard questions; he answers all of them, 'there was not any thing hid from the king.'
Solomon gives her 'of his royal bounty' whatever she desired, and she returns to her own country.

characters.name: Hadad the Edomite
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around a foreign adversary raised up against Solomon's later reign.

spouses: the sister of Tahpenes the queen (unnamed)
genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: 'Hadad' is also the name of an earlier Edomite king (Genesis 36:35-36) and appears as an element in other names (e.g. 'Ben-hadad,' 'son of Hadad') — this is the adversary of Solomon in chapter 11, a distinct individual. Described as 'of the king's seed in Edom' (11:14), fled to Egypt as a child during David/Joab's campaign against Edom (11:15-17).

funFacts: Found 'great favour in the sight of Pharaoh,' who gave him his wife's sister in marriage and land (11:19).
Returns to Edom to oppose Solomon only after hearing that both David and Joab were dead (11:21-22).

verses.note: Fled to Egypt as a young child when Joab's campaign killed every male in Edom.
Given the sister of queen Tahpenes to wife; she bears Genubath, whom Tahpenes weans in Pharaoh's own household among Pharaoh's sons.

Becomes 'an adversary to Israel' alongside Rezon, and 'abhorred Israel, and reigned over Syria' — this final clause's referent is grammatically ambiguous between Hadad and Rezon; treated here as most naturally following Rezon's Damascus kingship (see that entry).

characters.name: Genubath
characters.perkNote: Raised within Pharaoh's own household, extending Hadad's Egyptian ties.

genealogy.mother: the sister of Tahpenes the queen (unnamed)
genealogy.note: Named twice within the single verse 11:20, per the text.

funFacts: Weaned by Tahpenes herself in Pharaoh's house, and raised 'among the sons of Pharaoh' (11:20) — an Edomite child given full royal Egyptian upbringing.

verses.note: 'And the sister of Tahpenes bare him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house: and Genubath was in Pharaoh's household among the sons of Pharaoh.'

characters.name: Tahpenes
characters.perkNote: Raises Hadad's son as her own within the Egyptian royal house.

genealogy.note: Named as 'the queen' whose sister married Hadad; her own parentage is not given.

funFacts: Her sister is given to Hadad in marriage by Pharaoh, and Tahpenes personally weans and raises the resulting son, Genubath (11:19-20).

verses.note: 'And Hadad found great favour in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him to wife the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen.'

characters.name: Rezon the son of Eliadah
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around a rival kingdom rising on Solomon's border.

genealogy.note: No further genealogy given; his prior service is only that he fled from 'his lord Hadadezer king of Zobah' (11:23) — that Hadadezer is a separate figure from Hadad the Edomite despite the similar name, per the text's own distinct spelling and title.

funFacts: Gathers a band of men and becomes their captain after fleeing his former master, eventually seizing Damascus and reigning there (11:23-24).
Explicitly named 'an adversary of Israel...and he abhorred Israel, and reigned over Syria' (11:25) — founding the Aramean kingship line that later produces the Ben-hadads of chapters 15, 20, and 22.

verses.note: Flees from Hadadezer king of Zobah, gathers men, and takes Damascus.
Becomes an adversary to Israel 'all the days of Solomon.'

characters.name: Rehoboam
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus tied to Judah's continuity — the line that keeps the throne after the split.

genealogy.note: Only relationships stated within 1 Kings are asserted.

funFacts: Rejects the elders' counsel to lighten Israel's labor and instead threatens to make the burden heavier: 'my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions' (12:11).
His reign is marked by the building of 'high places, and images, and groves' and by the presence of sodomites in the land — explicit religious decline (14:22-24).

verses.note: The people ask him to lighten the heavy yoke his father Solomon put upon them.
Ten tribes revolt, crying 'To your tents, O Israel' — the kingdom splits.
Shishak king of Egypt invades in his 5th year and takes the treasures of the Temple and king's house.

characters.name: Jeroboam the son of Nebat
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around rapid rise to kingship, undercut by institutionalized idolatry.

genealogy.note: His mother is named only as 'Zeruah, a widow woman' (11:26) — included here as a bulk genealogical note rather than a separate character entry, per no differentiated action beyond the parentage statement.

funFacts: Was 'a mighty man of valour' and Solomon's own servant, put in charge of the labor force of the house of Joseph, before his rebellion (11:26-28).
Sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan specifically to keep the people from returning to worship at Jerusalem (12:26-29) — a political calculation stated explicitly in the text, not left implicit.

verses.note: Introduced as Solomon's servant who 'lifted up his hand against the king.'
'Behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt' — sets up the golden calves.
Reigned 22 years; died, succeeded by his son Nadab.

characters.name: Ahijah the Shilonite
characters.perkNote: First blesses, then curses Jeroboam's house — the curse is the lasting outcome.

genealogy.note: No genealogy given beyond his hometown, Shiloh.

funFacts: Tears his own new garment into twelve pieces and gives Jeroboam ten, symbolically granting him ten tribes (11:29-31).
Later, though blind with age, recognizes Jeroboam's disguised wife by the sound of her feet at the door (14:4-6) before pronouncing the death of her son and the destruction of Jeroboam's house.

verses.note: Tears the new garment into twelve pieces, gives Jeroboam ten, prophesying his kingship over ten tribes.
Prophesies the death of Jeroboam's son Abijah and the eventual cutting off of Jeroboam's entire house.

characters.name: Abijah, son of Jeroboam
characters.perkNote: His death fulfills Ahijah's prophecy, marking the start of Jeroboam's downfall.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: not the same person as Abijam, king of Judah (Rehoboam's son, called 'Abijah' in some manuscripts/Chronicles) — two different men in overlapping timeframes.

funFacts: Ahijah's prophecy states he is the only member of Jeroboam's house in whom 'some good thing toward the LORD God of Israel' is found (14:13) — an unusually specific mercy embedded within an otherwise total judgment.

verses.note: Falls sick, prompting Jeroboam to send his disguised wife to inquire of Ahijah.
Dies the moment his mother's feet cross the threshold of the house, exactly as Ahijah foretold.

characters.name: The man of God out of Judah
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around a prophetic sign fulfilled centuries later, undercut by his own disobedience.

genealogy.note: Left unnamed by the text itself; no personal name is given anywhere in 1 Kings 13.

funFacts: Prophesies by name that a future king 'Josiah' will burn the bones of idolatrous priests on this very altar (13:2) — a remarkably specific naming prophecy; its fulfillment is recorded roughly 300 years later in 2 Kings 23:15-16, a later book not indexed here.

Is killed by a lion after being deceived into eating bread in Bethel against the LORD's explicit command to him — yet the lion, strangely, does not eat the body or maul the donkey standing beside it (13:24-28).

verses.note: Cries against the altar at Bethel, giving the sign that it shall be rent and the ashes poured out.
Given explicit command from the LORD: eat no bread, drink no water, and return not by the way he came.
Killed by a lion on the road after being deceived into disobeying that command.

characters.name: The old prophet who dwelt in Bethel
characters.perkNote: Deceives the man of God, leading directly to his death.

children: sons who report the man of God's actions to him (13:11)
genealogy.note: Left unnamed by the text; his sons are also unnamed.

funFacts: Lies to the man of God, claiming an angel spoke to him by the word of the LORD — the text explicitly states 'he lied unto him' (13:18).
Afterward mourns him, buries him in his own grave, and instructs his sons to lay his own bones beside his when he dies (13:30-31).

verses.note: Follows and deceives the man of God into eating bread at his house, against the LORD's command.
Recognizes it as fulfillment of the LORD's word, retrieves and buries the body, mourns him.

characters.name: Asa
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around religious reform and defensive alliance-building.

genealogy.note: His grandmother Maachah is called 'his mother' in the text (see her own entry for the idiom explanation); his birth mother is not separately named in 1 Kings.

funFacts: 'His heart was perfect with the LORD all his days' (15:14) — one of the strongest positive assessments given to any king in the book.

Uses silver and gold from the Temple and his own house treasury to buy Ben-hadad I's help against Baasha, rather than trusting the LORD in battle — a choice later criticized in 2 Chronicles 16:7-9, not within 1 Kings itself.

verses.note: Does right in the eyes of the LORD, removes the sodomites, and puts away the idols his fathers made.
Sends treasure to Ben-hadad son of Tabrimon to break his league with Baasha.
In his old age, 'diseased in his feet.'

characters.name: Maachah
characters.perkNote: Deposed from the queen mother's position for idolatry.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION AND TEXTUAL NOTE: 'Maachah' is a repeat name across scripture (also a wife of David, a wife/queen of Rehoboam elsewhere, and other figures) — flagged explicitly. Within 1 Kings, the text calls her 'his mother' both regarding Abijam (15:2) and regarding Asa (15:10, 15:13); she was Abijam's actual mother and thus Asa's grandmother, continuing to hold the queen-mother ('gebirah') position into her grandson's reign — 'mother' functions here as an idiom for that royal office rather than a strict biological claim for Asa specifically.

funFacts: Deposed by her own grandson Asa specifically 'because she had made an idol in a grove' (15:13), which Asa then burns at the brook Kidron.

verses.note: Named as the mother of Abijam, 'the daughter of Abishalom.'
Removed by Asa 'from being queen' and her idol burnt.

characters.name: Ben-hadad (I), king of Syria, son of Tabrimon
characters.perkNote: Bought ally against Baasha — his help comes at the price of Temple treasure.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED, MAJOR: this is a distinct figure from the Ben-hadad of chapters 20 and 22 who leads the coalition of thirty-two kings against Ahab (see ben_hadad_ii_of_syria). The relationship between the two Ben-hadads is not stated outright by the text; 20:34 has the later Ben-hadad refer to cities 'my father took from thy father' regarding Omri, which implies he is a son or dynastic successor of an earlier Ben-hadad rather than certainly the same individual as this one — treated here as two separate entries given the roughly one-reign gap (Asa vs. Ahab) between their appearances, with the exact relationship left explicitly uncertain.

funFacts: Accepts Asa's silver and gold and breaks his existing league with Baasha, then captures several cities in northern Israel including Dan and all Naphtali (15:20).

verses.note: Receives Asa's treasure, breaks league with Baasha, smites Ijon, Dan, Abelbethmaachah, and all Naphtali.

characters.name: Baasha
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around usurpation followed by prophetic judgment.

genealogy.note: His father Ahijah is a different man from Ahijah the Shilonite the prophet — same name, unrelated figures.

funFacts: Conspires against Nadab while Nadab besieges the Philistine city Gibbethon, killing him and 'all the house of Jeroboam,' explicitly said to fulfill Ahijah's earlier word (15:27-29).

Ironically receives the identical judgment he himself carried out — Jehu son of Hanani condemns him for 'walking in the way of Jeroboam' and for killing him (16:1-4,7), and his own house is later wiped out by Zimri the same way.

verses.note: Conspires against Nadab and kills him at Gibbethon, reigning in his stead.
Kills all the house of Jeroboam, leaving him none remaining.
Dies and is succeeded by his son Elah.

characters.name: Nadab, son of Jeroboam
characters.perkNote: Assassinated by Baasha two years into his reign.

genealogy.note: No further genealogy given.

funFacts: Reigns only two years and is explicitly said to have 'walked in the way of his father, and in his sin' (15:26).

verses.note: Reigns two years over Israel; killed by Baasha at Gibbethon while besieging it.

characters.name: Jehu the son of Hanani
characters.perkNote: Delivers the prophetic word condemning Baasha's dynasty.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: this Jehu (a prophet, son of Hanani) is a different person from the later Jehu son of Nimshi, the military commander anointed king over Israel in 2 Kings 9 — same name, entirely different role and era, not to be conflated.

funFacts: His prophecy against Baasha (16:1-4) uses almost the exact same language Ahijah used against Jeroboam — dogs eating the dead, fowls eating the dead in the field — underscoring the book's repeating pattern of dynastic judgment.

verses.note: The word of the LORD comes to him against Baasha, condemning him for walking in Jeroboam's way.
Reiterates the judgment, also condemning Baasha specifically for killing the house of Jeroboam.

characters.name: Zimri
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around a brief, violent seizure of power.

genealogy.note: No genealogy given beyond his role as 'captain of half his chariots' under Elah (16:9).

funFacts: Kills Elah while he was 'drinking himself drunk' in the house of Arza, steward of his house, in Tirzah (16:9-10).
Reigns only seven days before, besieged in Tirzah by Omri's forces, he burns the king's house down over himself (16:15-18).

verses.note: Kills Elah and reigns in his stead.
Burns the king's house upon himself when the city is taken, and dies.

characters.name: Elah, son of Baasha
characters.perkNote: Assassinated by his own officer while drunk.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: distinct from the later Elah listed as father of the officer Shimei the son of Elah (4:18) — though note 4:18 occurs earlier in the book under Solomon's reign, so that Elah predates and is unrelated to this king Elah.

funFacts: Reigns only two years (16:8) before being killed.

verses.note: Reigns two years; killed by Zimri while drunk in Tirzah.

characters.name: Omri
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around dynasty-founding and city-building.

genealogy.note: No further genealogy given.

funFacts: Buys the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and builds the city that becomes Israel's capital, naming it after Shemer (16:24).
The text's summary judgment on him is unusually harsh in its brevity: he 'wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him' (16:25).

verses.note: Half the people follow Tibni, half follow Omri; Omri's faction prevails.
Reigns 12 years total; buys the hill of Samaria and builds the city.

characters.name: Tibni, the son of Ginath
characters.perkNote: Loses the succession struggle against Omri.

genealogy.note: No further detail given; the text does not state how he dies, only that 'Tibni died' (16:22).

funFacts: Half of Israel supported his claim to the throne against Omri's — a genuine civil-war-scale split, not a minor rivalry (16:21).

verses.note: Contests the throne with Omri; the people that followed Omri prevail, and Tibni dies.

characters.name: Ahab
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around wealth and military strength undercut by repeated moral failure.

genealogy.note: Only relationships stated within 1 Kings are asserted.

funFacts: Built 'an ivory house' and cities (22:39) — one of the wealthiest kings described in the book.
The text states he did evil 'above all that were before him' (16:30) — an even harsher formula than the one used for his own father Omri.
Sulks and refuses to eat after Naboth refuses to sell his vineyard, requiring Jezebel to act on his behalf (21:4-7).

verses.note: Marries Jezebel, serves Baal, and builds an altar and grove for Baal in Samaria.
Defeats Ben-hadad's first siege of Samaria.
Covets Naboth's vineyard; Jezebel orchestrates Naboth's death so Ahab can take it.
Killed in battle at Ramoth-gilead, struck by a bow drawn 'at a venture.'

characters.name: An unnamed prophet (advisor and later accuser of Ahab)
characters.perkNote: Advises the winning battle strategy against Syria, then turns to condemn Ahab for mercy shown afterward.

genealogy.note: Left unnamed by the text; it is not stated whether the prophet who advises the battle plan in 20:13-14 is the same one who condemns Ahab in 20:35-43, though the passage reads as continuous and is treated that way here.

funFacts: Uses a staged parable — disguising himself and getting another man to wound him — to trap Ahab into unknowingly pronouncing judgment on himself, the same device Nathan once used on David (though that earlier episode is in 2 Samuel, not this book).

verses.note: Comes to Ahab before the battle, telling him the LORD will deliver Ben-hadad's army into his hand.
Condemns Ahab, in parable form, for letting Ben-hadad go: 'thy life shall go for his life.'

characters.name: Jezebel
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around ruthless patronage of Baal worship and elimination of opposition.

genealogy.note: Only relationships stated within 1 Kings are asserted.

funFacts: 'Cut off the prophets of the LORD' — the specific act that forces Obadiah to hide 100 surviving prophets (18:4,13).
Forges letters in Ahab's name and seals them with his seal to orchestrate Naboth's judicial murder (21:8-10).
Her threat against Elijah — 'so let the gods do to me...if I make not thy life as the life of one of them' (19:2) — is what drives him to flee to Horeb.

verses.note: Introduced as the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, married to Ahab.
Cuts off the LORD's prophets, prompting Obadiah to hide 100 of them.
Writes letters in Ahab's name to have Naboth falsely accused and stoned.

characters.name: Naboth the Jezreelite
characters.perkNote: Refuses to sell his inheritance; his death becomes the pretext for its seizure.

genealogy.note: No genealogy given beyond his home in Jezreel.

funFacts: His refusal is grounded explicitly in inherited-land principle, not mere stubbornness: 'The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee' (21:3).

Falsely accused by two 'sons of Belial' of blaspheming God and the king, then stoned outside the city (21:10-13) — Elijah's subsequent condemnation of Ahab specifically invokes the place where 'dogs licked the blood of Naboth' (21:19).

verses.note: Refuses to sell or trade his vineyard to Ahab, citing his fathers' inheritance.
Stoned to death on false testimony procured by Jezebel.

characters.name: Elijah the Tishbite
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around dramatic prophetic confrontation and provision in scarcity.

genealogy.note: Only described as 'the Tishbite, who was of the inhabitants of Gilead' (17:1); no further genealogy given.

funFacts: Announces a drought 'according to my word' before it happens (17:1), then is fed by ravens at the brook Cherith (17:2-6).

At Carmel, has the prophets of Baal slain at the brook Kishon — the text specifies only 'the prophets of Baal' were taken and killed there (18:40); the 400 prophets of the groves (Asherah) invited earlier at Jezebel's table (18:19) are never explicitly stated to be present at the contest or executed alongside them.
Encounters the LORD at Horeb not in wind, earthquake, or fire, but in 'a still small voice' (19:11-12).

verses.note: Announces the drought to Ahab.
Challenges the people at Carmel: 'How long halt ye between two opinions?'
Has the prophets of Baal — specifically them, not the Asherah prophets — taken to Kishon and slain.
Encounters the LORD in the still small voice at Horeb.
Condemns Ahab over Naboth's death.

characters.name: The widow of Zarephath
characters.perkNote: Hosts and sustains Elijah through the drought; her household is sustained in turn.

genealogy.note: Neither she nor her son is given a personal name in the text.

funFacts: Her barrel of meal and cruse of oil do not run out for the duration of the drought, exactly as Elijah promises (17:14-16).
Her son dies and is revived by Elijah, who stretches himself upon the child three times (17:17-22) — one of the earliest resurrection accounts in the Hebrew scriptures.

verses.note: Shares her last meal with Elijah; her meal and oil are miraculously sustained.
Her son dies and is restored to life by Elijah.

characters.name: Obadiah, the governor of Ahab's house
characters.perkNote: Secretly preserves 100 of the LORD's prophets despite serving in Ahab's court.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: this Obadiah (governor of Ahab's house, 18:3) is a different person from the prophet Obadiah, author of the book of Obadiah — there is no textual link identifying them as the same man, and this Obadiah is one of several distinct figures in scripture sharing the name.

funFacts: Hides 100 prophets of the LORD by fifty in a cave and feeds them bread and water at his own risk, during Jezebel's purge (18:4,13).
Is explicitly described as one who 'feared the LORD greatly' despite his position within Ahab's household (18:3).

verses.note: Introduced as governor of Ahab's house, who feared the LORD greatly and hid 100 prophets.
Meets Elijah on the road and, after some hesitation for fear of Ahab, agrees to tell Ahab Elijah is present.

characters.name: Elisha the son of Shaphat
characters.perkNote: Called as Elijah's successor; his full ministry belongs to a later book.

genealogy.note: Only his calling within 1 Kings is asserted; his extensive later ministry is recorded in 2 Kings, not indexed here.

funFacts: Found plowing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah casts his mantle upon him (19:19).
Burns his plowing equipment and boils the oxen's flesh using the yokes as fuel before following Elijah (19:21) — a decisive, irreversible break with his old life.

verses.note: Called by Elijah casting his mantle on him; burns his oxen equipment and follows him as a servant.

characters.name: Ben-hadad, king of Syria (leader of the thirty-two kings)
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around massed but ultimately unstable foreign alliance.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED, MAJOR: this Ben-hadad, who besieges Samaria with thirty-two allied kings in chapter 20 and is understood to be the Syrian king whose war leads to Ahab's death in chapter 22, is a distinct figure from the Ben-hadad of 15:18 (son of Tabrimon, Asa's contemporary and paid ally against Baasha — see ben_hadad_i_of_syria). The text never explicitly states the exact relationship between the two; 20:34's reference to 'the cities which my father took from thy father' regarding Omri suggests this Ben-hadad's father warred with Omri's generation, which would place this Ben-hadad roughly a generation after the Ben-hadad of 15:18 — but the text does not name that father or resolve whether he is that same earlier Ben-hadad grown older, or a son/successor of the same dynastic name. Both are indexed here as separate managers to keep the reign chronology (Asa's era vs. Ahab's era) and the Kings review requirement for a distinct, fully-written entry for this antagonist clear and unambiguous.

funFacts: Gathers 'all his host together: and there were thirty and two kings with him' to besiege Samaria (20:1).
Demands Ahab's silver, gold, wives, and children be surrendered — then, when Ahab initially agrees, escalates the demand further, provoking the war he ultimately loses (20:2-6).
Spared by Ahab after defeat and released under a covenant of restored cities and trade rights in Damascus (20:32-34) — the mercy an unnamed prophet condemns Ahab for immediately afterward.

verses.note: Gathers his host and thirty-two allied kings to besiege Samaria.
His army is routed by Ahab; he escapes on a horse.
Surrenders and is spared by Ahab, who makes a covenant with him and lets him go.
Three years of peace between Syria and Israel follow before the war over Ramoth-gilead in which Ahab dies — the Syrian king is not renamed in ch. 22, understood as continuing from ch. 20.

characters.name: Jehoshaphat
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around cautious alliance-seeking and religious faithfulness.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: 'Jehoshaphat' is also the name of two of Solomon's officers within this same book — Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, the recorder (4:3), and Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, officer over Issachar (4:17) — three different men named Jehoshaphat appear across 1 Kings alone.

funFacts: 'Walked in all the ways of Asa his father; he turned not aside from it, doing that which was right in the eyes of the LORD' (22:43) — one of the more consistently positive assessments in the book.

Requests a true prophet of the LORD before joining Ahab's battle at Ramoth-gilead, specifically because he distrusts the 400 court prophets who unanimously promise victory (22:7) — this request is what brings Micaiah into the narrative.
Builds ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they are wrecked at Ezion-geber before sailing (22:48), after which he refuses a joint venture with Ahaziah of Israel (22:49).

verses.note: Succeeds Asa as king of Judah.
Asks whether there is a prophet of the LORD besides the 400, leading to Micaiah being summoned.
His Tarshish ships are wrecked; he declines Ahaziah's offer to sail together.

characters.name: Micaiah, the son of Imlah
characters.perkNote: Thematic bonus around a lone truthful prophet standing against a unanimous false consensus.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: 'Micaiah' is also spelled/rendered elsewhere for other figures (e.g. Micaiah/Maachah as a name-variant issue at 2 Chronicles 13:2, and other men named Micaiah in Jeremiah and Nehemiah) — this is the prophet son of Imlah in Ahab's court, a distinct individual not linked to those others by the text.

funFacts: Initially answers Ahab with sarcastic mimicry of the false prophets' message before Ahab presses him to 'tell me nothing but that which is true' (22:15-16).

Describes a vision of the LORD's council permitting a 'lying spirit' to go out and deceive Ahab's prophets specifically to entice him to his death at Ramoth-gilead (22:19-23) — an unusually candid depiction of divine permission for deception within a prophetic vision.
Struck on the cheek by Zedekiah son of Chenaanah and imprisoned on bread and water by Ahab's order for his unwelcome prophecy (22:24-27).

verses.note: Ahab names him: 'I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.'
Prophesies Israel 'scattered upon the hills, as sheep that have not a shepherd' — foretelling Ahab's death.
Imprisoned by Ahab's order after his prophecy.

characters.name: Zedekiah, the son of Chenaanah
characters.perkNote: Leads the 400 false court prophets and physically strikes Micaiah.

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: distinct from Zedekiah, the last king of Judah (2 Kings 24-25) — a much more prominent figure by the same name, entirely unrelated to this false court prophet.

funFacts: Makes 'horns of iron' as a theatrical prop, declaring Ahab will push the Syrians with them until consumed (22:11) — showmanship contrasted directly against Micaiah's plain vision.

verses.note: Makes horns of iron and prophesies false victory for Ahab.
Strikes Micaiah on the cheek and challenges him: 'Which way went the Spirit of the LORD from me to speak unto thee?'

characters.name: Abijam

genealogy.note: Reigns only briefly; called 'Abijah' in 2 Chronicles, a spelling variant of the same king not treated as a separate person.

funFacts: 'He walked in all the sins of his father...his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father' (15:3) — an explicit unfavorable comparison to David.

verses.note: Begins to reign over Judah; reigns three years.
War between him and Jeroboam continues throughout his reign.

characters.name: Ahaziah, son of Ahab

genealogy.note: His fuller narrative (illness, death) is recorded in 2 Kings 1, not this book; only his brief introduction here is indexed.

funFacts: Declines Jehoshaphat's refused offer to jointly send ships to Ophir (22:49) — the last verses of 1 Kings, ending the book on an unresolved note that continues into 2 Kings.

verses.note: Begins to reign over Israel; 'he served Baal, and worshipped him, and provoked to anger the LORD God of Israel.'

characters.name: Pharaoh's daughter

genealogy.note: No personal name given; identified only by her father's title.

funFacts: Given the city of Gezer as a dowry after Pharaoh personally burned and captured it from the Canaanites (9:16) — an unusually specific act of military conquest performed as a wedding gift.

Solomon builds her a separate house, stated because he considered the places David had lived too holy for a foreign wife to dwell in (2 Chronicles 8:11 gives this reasoning explicitly; 1 Kings 7:8 and 9:24 record only that the house was built, without stating that reasoning).

verses.note: Solomon makes affinity with Pharaoh and marries his daughter.
Given the city of Gezer as a dowry.
Listed first among the 'strange women' Solomon loved.

characters.name: Shishak, king of Egypt

genealogy.note: No genealogy given.

funFacts: Shelters Jeroboam as a fugitive from Solomon (11:40), then invades Jeroboam's own rival kingdom of Judah under Rehoboam just five years later (14:25) — backing both sides of the divided kingdom in turn.

verses.note: Solomon seeks to kill Jeroboam; Jeroboam flees to Shishak in Egypt.
Invades Jerusalem in Rehoboam's 5th year and takes the treasures of the Temple and king's house.

characters.name: Azariah, the son of Zadok

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: distinct from Azariah the son of Nathan (4:5), listed three verses later in the same officer roster — two different men named Azariah in Solomon's own administration.

funFacts: Listed first among Solomon's chief officers, holding the priesthood.

verses.note: 'Azariah the son of Zadok the priest' — first named in Solomon's officer list.

characters.name: Azariah, the son of Nathan

genealogy.father: Nathan (not stated to be Nathan the prophet)
genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: distinct from Azariah the son of Zadok (4:2). Also, this 'Nathan' is not stated by the text to be Nathan the prophet, though the name is shared — no textual link identifies them, so no identification is asserted here.

funFacts: Set 'over the officers' — administratively distinct from his near-namesake brother-officer Azariah son of Zadok, who held the priesthood.

verses.note: 'Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers.'

characters.name: Baana, the son of Ahilud

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: near-collision with Baanah the son of Hushai (4:16) in the same twelve-officer roster — different men, similar names. Shares a father's name, Ahilud, with Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud the recorder (4:3); the text does not state they are brothers, though it is plausible given the shared patronymic — hedged, not asserted.

funFacts: Assigned Taanach and Megiddo and all Bethshean as his district (4:12) — a large, strategically important territory.

verses.note: Lists his district: Taanach, Megiddo, and all Bethshean.

characters.name: Baanah, the son of Hushai

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: near-collision with Baana the son of Ahilud (4:12) in the same roster. Not stated to be the same Hushai as David's counselor (2 Samuel 15) — no textual link given.

funFacts: Assigned Asher and Aloth as his district (4:16).

verses.note: 'Baanah the son of Hushai was in Asher and in Aloth.'

characters.name: Jehoshaphat, the son of Ahilud

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED, TRIPLE: 1 Kings contains three different men named Jehoshaphat — this recorder (4:3), the officer Jehoshaphat son of Paruah (4:17), and Jehoshaphat king of Judah (his own manager tier). None are the same person.

funFacts: Holds the role of 'recorder,' a senior administrative post, distinct from the scribes Elihoreph and Ahiah mentioned in the same verse.

verses.note: 'Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, the recorder.'

characters.name: Jehoshaphat, the son of Paruah

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: see Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud's entry — three distinct Jehoshaphats appear in this book.

funFacts: Assigned Issachar as his district (4:17).

verses.note: 'Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar.'

characters.name: Shimei, the son of Elah

genealogy.note: NAMING COLLISION FLAGGED: distinct from Shimei the son of Gera, executed by Solomon (2:36-46, see that entry) — both named Shimei within the same book. His father Elah is also a different figure from Elah son of Baasha, the later king of Israel.

funFacts: Assigned Benjamin as his district (4:18).

verses.note: 'Shimei the son of Elah, in Benjamin.'

genealogyLists.solomons_twelve_officers_partial_bulk_li: Several of Solomon's twelve district officers (4:7-19) have no differentiated action beyond their name/patronymic and district, and are listed here rather than as full character entries: Ben-hur in mount Ephraim (4:8); Ben-deker in Makaz, Shaalbim, Bethshemesh, and Elonbethhanan (4:9); Ben-hesed in Aruboth, including Sochoh and all Hepher (4:10); Ben-abinadab in all the region of Dor, who 'had Taphath the daughter of Solomon to wife' (4:11) — a differentiated marriage detail, noted here though he lacks further action; Ben-geber in Ramothgilead, with the towns of Jair the son of Manasseh in Gilead and the region of Argob (4:13); Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim (4:14); Ahimaaz in Naphtali, who 'also took Basmath the daughter of Solomon to wife' (4:15) — the second officer-marriage detail; Geber the son of Uri, in the country of Gilead (4:19), described as 'the only officer which was in the land.' Baana/Baanah, the two Jehoshaphats, the two Azariahs, and Shimei son of Elah from this same roster are promoted to individual 'named' character entries above due to the naming-collision flags required by this pass.
genealogyLists.solomons_wives_and_concubines: 1 Kings 11:1-3 states Solomon had 700 wives, princesses, and 300 concubines, drawn from Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Zidonian, and Hittite women, with no individual names given beyond Pharaoh's daughter and Naamah the Ammonitess (mother of Rehoboam, named at 14:21). Not enumerated individually here per methodology on undifferentiated bulk lists.
genealogyLists.obadiahs_hidden_prophets: 1 Kings 18:4,13 states Obadiah hid 'an hundred prophets' of the LORD by fifty in a cave; none are individually named.

notes:
CORRECTED SECOND-PASS REDRAFT of 1 Kings, built from scratch per the six flagged first-draft issues:

(1) SCHEMA FIX: the chapters 20/22 antagonist now has a full character entry (ben_hadad_ii_of_syria, role manager) matching its scribeTier managerId — verified no scribeTier or parentManagerId in this draft points to a missing id. Final cross-reference check performed: every managerId in scribeTiers (22 entries) has a matching characters[] id with role manager or law; every parentManagerId (18 submanager entries) points to a characters[] id with role manager. No orphaned references found.

(2) Hadad the Edomite's genealogy.children now includes "Genubath" (named twice in 11:20, both instances cited), and Tahpenes has her own full submanager entry (raised Genubath in Pharaoh's household).

(3) Azariah the son of Zadok (4:2) and Azariah the son of Nathan (4:5) both given individual 'named' entries with explicit collision flags cross-referencing each other.

(4) Baana the son of Ahilud (4:12) and Baanah the son of Hushai (4:16) both given individual 'named' entries with explicit near-collision flags cross-referencing each other. (A bonus, not-in-the-list collision was also caught during the self-scan: THREE different Jehoshaphats appear in this book alone — the king, the recorder son of Ahilud (4:3), and the officer son of Paruah (4:17) — all three flagged.)

(5) Hiram the craftsman's entry uses ONLY 1 Kings 7:13-14's actual KJV wording ('a widow's son of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in brass') — the NIV/ESV-style 'Huram-abi' rendering is not used anywhere, and the entry does not draw on 2 Chronicles phrasing at all.

(6) Elijah's Carmel entry (18:40) states only that 'the prophets of Baal' were taken to Kishon and slain, with an explicit note that the 400 Asherah/grove prophets invited in 18:19 are never stated to be present at the contest or executed — ambiguity flagged rather than silently resolved.

ADDITIONAL NAMING COLLISIONS CAUGHT IN THIS PASS (beyond the required list): Shimei son of Gera (executed by Solomon, ch. 2) vs. Shimei son of Elah (officer, 4:18); Jehu son of Hanani (prophet vs. Baasha) vs. the later Jehu son of Nimshi (2 Kings 9, outside this book but flagged to prevent future conflation); Zedekiah son of Chenaanah (false prophet, ch. 22) vs. Zedekiah the last king of Judah; Abijah son of Jeroboam (ch. 14) vs. Abijam/Abijah king of Judah; Elah son of Baasha (king) vs. Elah (father of officer Shimei, 4:18); Ben-hadad I (Asa's era, 15:18) vs. Ben-hadad II (Ahab's era, ch. 20/22) — the relationship between the two is explicitly hedged as textually unresolved rather than asserted as same-person or clean father/son.

PROMOTIONS beyond a strict minor/major split, per methodology point 3 (load-bearing test): Adonijah, Jezebel, Hadad the Edomite, Rezon, and Jehoshaphat were each given their own full manager tier rather than folded in as submanagers, because removing any of them would change a major plot outcome (succession crisis, Naboth's death and Elijah's flight, two distinct foreign adversaries against Solomon, and the Ramoth-gilead campaign/Micaiah episode respectively).

HYBRID CONTENT: only one law-type tier was used (temple_dedication_and_covenant, ch. 8-9) — the temple's physical CONSTRUCTION (ch. 6-7) was kept character-driven under Solomon/Hiram/Hiram-the-craftsman since those persons are personally embodied (acting, building, negotiating), while the DEDICATION PRAYER and the LORD's covenant response are pure thematic/covenantal instruction with clear deliveredBy attribution, fitting the law-tier definition.

Not built as full entries, and explicitly not invented: individual names for Solomon's 700 wives/300 concubines, Obadiah's 100 hidden prophets, and most of the twelve district officers with no differentiated action beyond name+district (all logged in genealogyLists instead, per methodology point 8).
